en: *The Two Gates of Resolving Doubts and Cultivating Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land*, composed by the Śramaṇa Zunshe of Mount Qi during the Song Dynasty.
The precious realm of An-yang (Sukhāvatī) is praised by the Great Awakened One; those of the three grades ascend loftily, conceiving the golden lotus at dusk.
The arrayed constellations still feel ashamed before a drop of ocean water;
the morning stroll by the jade pond and the World-Lamp are but forced metaphors for the sands of the Ganges.
This is truly because:
Coming from the ten directions and proceeding for the benefit of the four modes of birth,
though you radiate light universally,
they ultimately bow their heads in individual pursuit.
Therefore, when observing from the present back to antiquity, both in the land of India and the Imperial Capital [China],
there were great sages and supreme saints who all composed elegant prose as covenant texts— such as Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Vasubandhu, and Nāgārjuna, among the ranks of holy sages.
There are also separate translations of the vow-texts,
or those recorded in other sutras and treatises which are not fully included here.
This [vow], moreover, was composed with the brush by the eminent scholar Jue De, who was a leading figure among the followers of the Pure Society at Donglin during the Jin dynasty.
The eighteen worthies, including Liu Lei, along with one hundred and twenty-three others, made a collective vow.
Subsequently, the lay elite and monks of esteemed virtue and reputation composed the words of this testament.
The customs of those who purify their aspirations abound in written records;
observing this present dedication, the succession of chants and responses continues one after another.
Truly, this constitutes the thoroughfare of the Way and its Virtue.
They are those who always delight in straightforward salvation.

Yet, in this world, many who have merely received the initial tonsure and the cutting of their robes do not recognize the cardinal directions; when suddenly encountering one who asks for guidance, they feel no shame in their pretentious blustering, or even roll up their sleeves to dismiss [the Dharma] as a minor teaching.
Some laugh loudly and dismiss it as a provisional vehicle (*upāyayāna*),
because their words contradict the scriptures and cause people to be confused regarding the eternal canons.
Does the *I Ching* not say:
If one dwells in their chamber and utters words that are not good,
those beyond a thousand li will go against them;
how much more so those who are near?
I have thus briefly set forth these two gates: Resolving Doubts about Rebirth in the Pure Land and the Practice of Vows.

I am ashamed that my phrasing lacks literary elegance, yet I hope the substance of the principles may remain. May those who can distinguish between beans and wheat take note, and may those who can discern between the Jing and Wei rivers forever maintain their distinction.
He cut down the stinking forest of *eranda* and planted the fragrant trunks of *candana*.
From the beginning to the end of faith, understanding, practice, and vows, this work does not exceed several thousand words.
That which can fully encompass [the path] is indeed these two gates.
The first is the Gate for Resolving Doubts, consisting of: (1) doubt regarding the teacher, and (2) doubt regarding the Dharma.
The third section, "Doubting Oneself," consists of three parts: first, the gate of worship and repentance;
second, the gate of recitation;
and third, the gate of binding the object of focus.
Regarding the first "Gate of Resolving Doubts" among the fourfold assembly’s gates of merit:
doubt acts as an obstacle to faith,
such that even small worldly virtues cannot be brought to fruition.
How much more so for the Great Path of Bodhi!
Someone said:
"The Tiantai Master Zhiyi has already provided an exposition on the *Shiyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Ten Doubts)."
What need is there for this text?
Nevertheless, it is briefly composed from three perspectives:
first, to inspire faith and joy in kings, ministers, and officials.
Due to the scarcity of leisure amidst many duties, it is difficult to seek out extensive texts.
Therefore, I shall now set forth the general outline and briefly describe the modes of manifestation,
so that they may be easily consulted.
Because it is easy to practice.
Second, within this treatise, most difficult points are explained according to specific matters;
only the second and third [sections] briefly establish them by relying on principle.
Furthermore, since phenomena are inexhaustible, doubts regarding them are likewise unfathomable.
Now, I shall simply clarify a single principle as the source of all dharmas;
once the source is pointed out, the flow can be understood.
Third, as for those who speak directly against [the teaching]:
they contradict the scriptures and deviate from reason, thereby harming themselves and others.
Thus, regarding the second category, those who harbor doubts about the Dharma—
I have selected the essential from the minor and grasped the great to clarify the provisional and the real,
so that those who come may not be confused.
As for Master Dao’an’s *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth) in six fascicles:
The *Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Various Doubts) in seven fascicles by Dharma Master Huai’gan;
the *Anle ji* (Anthology on Peaceful Bliss) in three fascicles by Meditation Master Daochuo;
and the *Jingtu cibei ji* (Anthology on Compassion for the Pure Land) in three fascicles by Tripiṭaka Master Cimin.
The two-fascicle *Jingtu ji* (Anthology on the Pure Land) by Zen Master Enchin.
Among the various masters of past and present who have turned their hearts toward the Pure Land realm,
some have composed commentaries to explain the sutras.
Some establish treatises based on the sūtras;
some explain difficult points according to their own inclinations;
and some offer praise through gāthās.
Although these various paths lead to the same destination, each presents its own views;
thus, they fill volumes upon volumes, making it difficult to investigate them thoroughly.
Now, I have unified those hundred schools under three categories of doubt, encompassing them all.
However, these words are derived from the *Tiantai Zhiguan* (The Great Calming and Contemplation) and are not spoken from mere conjecture.
First is doubt regarding the teacher;
second is doubt regarding the Dharma.
Third is doubting oneself.
First, regarding doubting the teacher:
there are two kinds of teachers.
First, the teachers of heterodox and external paths,
who delude people with inverted views, are not those from whom one should receive the teachings.
Second, the teachers of the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there are causes and fruits pertaining to both ordinary beings and sages;
it is possible for ordinary beings and those at the stage of the cause not yet to have attained full realization,
just as Candrakīrti asserted that Maitreya is not yet an omniscient one (sarvajña).
This refers precisely to the saying: "Wait until after the Way of the Dragon Flower [Buddha] to once again seek the ford.
It is now revealed that the Western [Pure Land] is for the purpose of causing those who practice dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*) to turn toward it.
Only the Buddhas, the holy teachers who are the ultimate fruit—
Śākyamuni Tathāgata and all the Buddhas of the ten directions—
extend their broad and long tongues and speak words of truth.
Since it is praised and one is encouraged to be reborn there,
what further cause for confusion could there be?
Second, as for doubting the Dharma:
The Buddha-dharma consists of two types:
first, the provisional teachings of the Hīnayāna;
second, the definitive teachings of the Mahāyāna.
Within the Mahāyāna, there are further distinctions between the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
What is now discussed regarding the Pure Land is the Dharma that is the most definitive among the definitive meanings of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntika school of the Hīnayāna exhaustively encompasses all the scriptural volumes (peṭaka),
yet not a single word therein praises or encourages rebirth in a pure land in another direction.
Thus, Vasubandhu’s treatise states:
"Women and those with impaired faculties do not give rise to the seeds of the two vehicles.
This is the explicit scriptural evidence.
[The opponent] asks regarding the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra* and other texts.
All [scriptures] state that in that land there are śrāvaka disciples;
furthermore, the Drum-Resounding King Sūtra (Dharmarāja-saṃgīti-sūtra) says:
"The name of the Buddha’s mother is Viśeṣacārumatī."
There should also be women present. [The interlocutor] replies:
"The Buddha’s mother likely refers to the time of his initial descent from the Tuṣita heaven;
once he had attained perfect enlightenment, the land was purified accordingly."
There must be no woman who is her mother;
she may instead be transformed into a male,
as was the case with this dragon girl.
Alternatively, regarding the case of passing away as with the mother of Siddhārtha,
some commentators cite this scriptural passage and claim that there are women in that land; however, this is incorrect.
The Śrāvakas have been reconciled according to the *Sūtra Commentary* and the *Treatise on the Ten Doubts*.
Now, to clarify the Mahāyāna, there are further three types.
The first is the common teaching of the Three Vehicles (*tri-yāna*).
Thus, although this gate is generally open to the Mahāyāna, it is closely associated with the two vehicles; furthermore,
it pertains to the bodhisattvas of this specific teaching,
who, though transforming others and purifying buddha-fields, [remain within this scope].
When their transformation is complete, they return to the same state as those of the two vehicles, merging into ultimate extinction.
The profound principle of the Pure Land is not known by them;
it is not of definitive meaning for them.
Second is the distinct teaching of the Mahāyāna.
This clarifies the unique bodhisattva dharma of the Mahāyāna;
although it discusses the ultimate truth, one realizes the fruition only after the path.
If one does not realize the fusion with the Pure Land, one stands outside the principle;
if the myriad dharmas are accomplished through cultivation, they do not arise from the inherent possession within the mind.
Thus, even if one practices the Way for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust and travels extensively through Buddha-fields, [the goal remains unattained].
To point toward that Pure Land as cause and effect is merely an expedient means external to the essence; this,
too, is not yet fully understood.
Third is the Perfect Teaching of the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*).
The purport of this teaching is that cause and effect are perfectly interfused,
suddenly perfecting the subtlety of the Buddha-dharma.
Beyond this, there is no further scope for deliberation.
As the Sūtra says:
"If one seeks thoroughly throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle."
This is what is meant by the "One Buddha Vehicle.
It is the Great Vehicle within the Great Vehicle,
and the definitive meaning within the definitive meaning.
The pure and impure lands of the ten directions are gathered within a single moment;
in one thought, the entirety of form and mind is arrayed and fully encompassed within the Dharma-realm.
All of these are inherently possessed by the celestial nature from the beginning, rather than being newly formed through dependent origination.
Since it is so for a single thought-moment, it is likewise so for a single atom;
thus, within each and every atom are all lands,
and within each and every mind are all minds.
Each and every mental object, in turn, pervades all others;
layer upon layer, they are inexhaustible and without obstruction,
manifesting all at once and suddenly, neither hidden nor revealed.
All are perfectly accomplished, without superiority or inferiority;
like a divine pearl suddenly containing all manner of jewels,
they are like Indra’s net, where a thousand lights reflect one another.
Since my mind has thus given rise to the realization that it is equal to the body of a Buddha,
only then do I truly understand that my spirit returns to billions of lands to truly take birth there.
How could it escape the fact that the essence conceived within my own heart is the ninefold lotus?
If, within the span of a single kṣaṇa, phenomena and principle were separated or purity and impurity were mutually obstructive,
how could ordinary people who have committed the five heinous crimes ascend to the Jewel Land through ten recitations,
or how could the worthy ones of the Two Vehicles who turn their minds toward enlightenment immediately reach the Golden Pond? How indeed could this be?
If one has faith in this perfect teaching, there is no phenomenon that will not be understood;
if one is ignorant of this ultimate principle, one will be deluded in every encounter with things.
Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
The mind is like a skilled painter,
creating the various five aggregates within all worlds.
There is nothing that is not created by the mind; this "creation" (zào) encompasses two types.
First, there is "inherent creation" (lìjù míng zào), wherein the ten realms of existence, both the environment and its inhabitants, are instantaneously complete within a single thought-moment.
Second, transformation and arising are termed "creation.
When one fully understands the principle of dependent origination—that there is nothing that is not brought about—one realizes that as it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha;
as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings.

Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction; it is precisely because they are non-distinct that the path of mutual resonance between response and stimulus can be established.
Through the mutual embrace of compassionate vows, both the collective transformation and individual transformations of cause and effect are thereby accomplished.
If one merely knows a single principle without realizing its non-differentiation,
yet fails to understand that all phenomena mutually contain one another, then one has not yet mastered the profound meaning of perfect interfusion.
Furthermore, the *Awakening of Faith* states:

"That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings. This directly points to the ordinary mind; this very mind encompasses all the six realms of the mundane world and the four realms of the supramundane Dharma of the noble ones.
The summary of the meaning is also twofold: first, inherent principle; second, constructed phenomena. Both together encompass the ten realms.

Within these ten realms—whether they be bodies or lands, pure or impure—there is no dharma that is not included. Based upon this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna (the Great Vehicle) is revealed. If it were not for this mind, how could one possibly be conveyed by it?
The *Sixteen Contemplations* states:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the body of the Dharma-realm;
they enter into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings."
"Up to the point that this mind creates the Buddha, this mind is the Buddha.
Furthermore, the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* says:
"The Buddha is my mind; it is by means of my mind that I see the Buddha."
Regarding such statements as "It is my mind that creates the Buddha," those who discuss this principle can find it clearly set forth throughout the volumes of the Mahāyāna.
As for the wondrous section of the Lotus Sūtra,
the Tathāgata personally recorded the rebirth [in Sukhāvatī];
in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the sudden teaching, Samantabhadra himself presented the dedication of merit.
Thus we know that while Amitābha was on the stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*),
he contemplated this principle and made great vows to universally embrace all beings;
now that Śākyamuni has attained fruition, he accords with this principle and praises it profoundly with his wide tongue.
Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, it is universally so.
Regarding the wondrous principle explained above as being perfectly consummate:
must all worldly people necessarily undergo contemplative practice before they can be born [in that state]?

Answer: This is not so. Here, we shall simply resolve your doubts directly, so that you may understand the adornments of the hundred jewels in the Pure Land and the causes and effects of the nine grades of rebirth.
Furthermore, within the slightest thought of every sentient being,
it is only when the fundamental nature is fully present that rebirth can be attained today;
through the power of their vows, the practical application of this rebirth occurs spontaneously.
This means that while pervading the ten directions, one does not depart from the present moment;
traversing the dharma-realm, one perfectly accords with the principle that all is but mind.
Thus, one avoids falling into the common stream of belief and clinging to this [view].
This is not the characteristic of their practice and vows;
it pertains precisely to the subsequent section and is not the subject here. Furthermore, one might ask:
since the characteristics of birth in each of the nine grades each have their own distinct types of practice?
The three grades of the superior class require both understanding and practice;
thus the text says:
"You practice the Mahāyāna and understand the ultimate truth."
He was indeed that very person.
If scholars of today were to see the worthy and strive for equality with them,
they would aspire to ascend the golden throne.
It relies solely upon sublime contemplation.
As for those of middling and inferior capacities— the causes for birth in the six realms—
they merely consist of scrupulously maintaining the prohibitive precepts and practicing benevolence in the world.
Even those of the lowest-of-the-low grade of birth who were originally rebellious and evil can be born in that land through ten moments of sincere mindfulness.
As long as one knows that the Pure Land exists, everyone is capable of turning their mind [toward it].
If this were not the case,
how could there be room for the distinctions and gradations of the nine ranks? Although worldly people may claim that the Pure Land arises from the Mahāyāna teachings,
they are unable to discern and differentiate them according to the aforementioned provisional and definitive teachings.
To merely escape confusion and ambiguity is not sufficient to resolve doubts.
Regarding the third doubt concerning oneself,
the question is as follows:
I am a commoner of the ordinary stage, entangled by worldly conditions and obscured by defilements.
How can this body be born in the various pure lands,
enter the ocean of worthies and sages, and become part of the assembly of those fixed in right concentration?
The commentary states:
If one thoroughly understands that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as described above is empty and pervasive,
and has faith in Amitābha’s fundamental vow to embrace and sustain sentient beings.
If one merely exerts oneself in meritorious deeds, why wait for guidance?
How much more so for those who achieve rebirth through ten recitations—
provided they have not committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the True Dharma.
Furthermore, even those with a concentrated mind who harbor ten thoughts of slanderous denial can be reborn there;
fortunately, we are now free from such evil,
and we instead sincerely aspire for rebirth through right vows.
What confusion could there be?
Regarding the second gate, the Gate of the Correct Practice of Vows,
it is briefly opened into four sections.
First is the gate of prostration and repentance;
second is the gate of ten recitations;
third is the gate of binding the object of focus.
Fourth are the gates of manifold merit.
As for why there are only four gates:
the complete and perfect cultivation of practice requires only these four.
What is this? First, one pays homage to the Buddha and performs repentance;
thus, having purified and removed karmic obstructions, the body and mind become bright and pure.
Therefore, the first gate is like a pure and fertile field.
Next, one cultivates the ten recitations with a concentrated mind to perfect the practice.
One establishes vows and sets a formal commitment to plant the primary cause for rebirth.
Therefore, the second section is like the seeds [of the preceding].
Next, one causes the mind to be focused on cherishing, protecting, nurturing, and causing the sprouts and stalks to flourish;
thus, the third gate is like pouring down a rain of fat.
Subsequently, one relies upon various merits as assistance to cause them to grow luxuriantly.
To cause them to quickly bear flowers and fruit,
the fourth gate is like pouring rich fat [upon a tree]. Thus,
it is known that one who is able to fully cultivate these four practices...
It is most supreme and most excellent.
Nevertheless, although such are the characteristics of the conditions,
if there is even a slight amount of leisure, [one should practice].
As for those who practice three, two, or even one [of the four practices],
they all will be born in that land,
because within each of the four gates there are specific practices and vows.
This is because these are all the direct causes.
Furthermore, one may also cultivate the methods of ritual and repentance on the six fast days,
and practice the method of ten recitations every day.
Since these ten recollections are the essential and most vital causes for purification, they must never be abandoned.
As for the latter two gates, one may practice them according to one's capacity;
otherwise, one may simply follow whatever one desires.
The four gates for practicing at will shall now be explained.
First, regarding the gate of prostration and repentance:
one should, every morning, perform this within the regular place of practice (dōjō) where offerings are made.
With one's head-dress and garments neat and dignified, and with a mind of solemn reverence,
one should personally burn incense before the Buddha image,
join the palms, settle the mind, and perform this [rite].
The chant proclaims:

"With all reverence and single-minded devotion, we prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem; with our hearts, we universally pay homage to all the Buddhas, Dharmas, and Sanghas of the ten directions and the three periods of time."
Having prostrated, they rise with both knees touching the ground,
holding incense burners and burning various kinds of famous incense,
and chant, saying:
"May these clouds of incense smoke pervade the worlds of the ten directions;
may the boundless Buddha-fields be adorned with immeasurable fragrances.

Having chanted this verse for the fulfillment of the Bodhisattva path and the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s fragrance, settle the mind in silent contemplation for a short while and universally offer clouds of incense to the Triple Gem."
The fragrance universally permeates all sentient beings, causing them all to conceive the thought of the Pure Land.
Having placed the incense burner, one performs a single prostration.
Rising, one joins the palms and bows the body with earnest devotion, visualizing that one is facing Amitābha and all the Buddhas.
And he praised him, saying:
The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body Is peerless and incomparable in the world;
It is inconceivable. Therefore, I now prostrate at his feet.
The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise so;
all phenomena are eternally abiding. Therefore, I take refuge in him who possesses great wisdom and the power of great vows, universally delivering all living beings.
May they cause me to cast off this body of feverish affliction And be born in that land of cool purity.
Now that I have purified my three karmas, I take refuge and offer praise;
May I, together with all sentient beings, Be born equally in the Land of Peace and Bliss. (Praise and Vow)
Having done so, he immediately prostrated before the Buddha.

With single-minded devotion, he addressed each one, chanting: "With all my heart, I pay homage to Amitābha Tathāgata of the Constantly Quiescent Light Pure Land, the pure and wondrous Dharma-body that pervades the entire Dharma-realm; with all my heart, I pay homage to the Real Reward Adorned [Land]."

With one mind, all Buddhas throughout the Dharma-realm pay homage to the Tathāgata Amitābha of the Western Land of Peace and Bliss, whose body of ocean-like subtle dust-marks pervades the Dharma-realm;

with one mind, all Buddhas throughout the Dharma-realm pay homage to the Tathāgata Amitābha of the Western Land of Peace and Bliss, whose body adorned with the marks of liberation pervades the Dharma-realm;

with one mind, all Buddhas throughout the Dharma-realm pay homage to the Tathāgata Amitābha of the Western Land of Peace and Bliss, whose body of the Mahāyāna faculty-realm pervades [the Dharma-realm].
With one mind, all Buddhas of the Dharma-realm prostrate to the Tathāgata Amitābha of the Western Land of Peace and Bliss,
whose emanated bodies pervade the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm. With one mind,
all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas whose bodies of purple-gold reach into the billions and pervade the entire Dharma-realm prostrate to the West.
With single-minded devotion, they prostrate to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the Western Land of Peace and Bliss— the Great Power Bodhisattva and the Boundless Light Wisdom-Body Bodhisattvas—
whose bodies pervade the Dharma-realm; they then kneel upon both knees before the assembly of holy ones in the pure great ocean of the West,
whose bodies of twofold adornment are perfected and who pervade the Dharma-realm.

Holding an incense burner and burning incense, with utmost sincerity, he uttered these words: "I now universally act for the sake of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm;
may they all vow to sever the three obstacles and take refuge in repentance. Having risen to prostrate, he knelt again upon the ground.
Holding the hand-incense burner, chant:
"With a sincere heart, I repent.
I, disciple [Name], and all sentient beings of the Dharma realm..."
Since beginningless time,
shrouded by ignorance and deluded by perversion,
they have practiced unwholesome dharmas through the six sense faculties and the three karmic actions.
They have extensively committed all manner of offenses, including the ten unwholesome actions and the five deeds of immediate retribution;
these are immeasurable, boundless, and cannot be fully described.
The Buddhas of the ten directions are always present in the world.
The sound of the Dharma never ceases;
wondrous fragrances fill all space;
the flavor of the Dharma abounds throughout the void.
Pure radiance is emitted, illuminating and touching all things;
the eternally abiding wondrous principle pervades the entirety of empty space.
Since beginningless time, I...
The six sense organs are internally blind and the three karmas are shrouded in darkness;
they neither see, nor hear, nor perceive, nor know.
Due to these causes and conditions, they flow long through birth and death, traversing the evil realms.
For hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, there will never be a time of emergence.
As the Sūtra says:
"Vairocana pervades all places."
The dwelling place of that Buddha is named Constantly Quiescent Light;
therefore, one should know that there are no dharmas whatsoever that are not the Buddha-dharma.
Yet I do not understand this, and thus I flow along with ignorance.
Thus, one perceives impurity within awakening and gives rise to fetters within liberation;
it is only now that one has begun to awaken to this.
Now, for the first time, I repent.
In the presence of all Buddhas and the World-Honored One Amitābha, I openly confess and repent.
May it cause my own three karmas and six sense faculties, as well as those of all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, [to be purified].
Whatever has been done, is being done, or will be done since beginningless time— whether committed by oneself, incited in others, or rejoiced in upon seeing or hearing it—
whether remembered or not.
Whether recognized or unrecognized,
whether doubted or not doubted,
whether concealed or exposed.
All grave offenses are ultimately purified.
Having completed my repentance,
the six faculties and three karmas are pure and free from blemish or defilement.
All the roots of goodness they cultivate are likewise pure;
they dedicate them all toward adorning the Pure Land,
so that they may universally be born together with all sentient beings in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
May Amitābha Buddha constantly come to protect and sustain me,
causing my roots of goodness to manifest and increase,
so that I do not lose the pure cause.
At the moment of death, their body and mind shall be possessed of right mindfulness;
their sight and hearing shall be clear and distinct,
as they behold Amitābha Buddha and his assembly of holy ones face-to-face.
Holding a flower pedestal, he welcomed me;
in a single kṣaṇa, I was born before the Buddha.
Having fulfilled the bodhisattva path, extensively delivered sentient beings, and together attained the wisdom of all modes, I performed repentance and made vows.
One should take refuge in and pay homage to Amitābha Buddha and all the Three Jewels; this should be recited three times.
If time is short or circumstances are urgent, it may be recited once.
Next, perform the ritual of circumambulation, either three times or seven times.
Recite this up to many times, calling out with the mouth:

"Namo Amitābha Buddha; Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva; Namo Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva; Namo to the assembly of pure great ocean-like Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas," whether three times, seven times, or more.
Recite in this manner as desired,
without restriction on the number of repetitions.
Next, before the Buddha, perform the threefold refuge.
Chanting: "I take refuge in the Buddha; may all sentient beings realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
I take refuge in the Dharma; may all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, their wisdom like the ocean."
Taking refuge in the Sangha, one should wish that all sentient beings preside over great assemblies without any hindrance; I pay homage to the noble assembly.
Next, proceed to a separate seat to recite sutras, such as the *Amitābha Sūtra* or the *Sūtra on the Sixteen Contemplations*.
If one is unable to recite the scriptural text at all,
one should single-mindedly invoke the name of Amitābha Buddha for a measured period of time and then cease.
Alternatively, it is also permissible to perform the dedication by summarizing [the merits].
Regarding the twentieth gate of recollection:
every morning, after one has finished dressing and preparing for the day.
Facing west and standing upright with palms joined, recite the name of Amitābha Buddha with a continuous voice;
one full breath constitutes one thought-moment (*ekacitta*).
Ten such breaths are called the ten recitations (*daśanāman*).
One should simply follow the length of the breath without limiting the number of Buddhas;
whether long or enduring, the breath reaching its limit constitutes the measure.
The sound of the Buddhas' voices should be neither too high nor too low.
Neither lax nor hurried, one maintains a balanced middle course.
In this way, the ten breaths are connected in an uninterrupted succession.
This is intended so that the mind does not scatter, taking focused diligence as the primary practice.
This is called "ten recollections" (daśa-smṛti) to show that it relies on the breath to bind the mind.
Having performed this recollection, [one proceeds].
The vow and dedication state:
"I, disciple [Name], single-mindedly take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
I pray that you will illuminate me with your pure light and embrace me with your compassionate vows."
Now, with right mindfulness, I have recited the name of the Tathāgata for the duration of ten recitations.
For the sake of the path to Bodhi, I seek birth in the Pure Land.
According to the Buddha’s original vow: "If there are sentient beings who wish to be born in my land..."
If, with a sincere heart of faith and joy, one recites this even ten times,
yet I do not attain perfect enlightenment, may I not become a Buddha—
except for those who have committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the true Dharma.
I now recall from my birth until this moment that I have neither committed the five heinous crimes nor slandered the Mahāyāna.
May these ten recollections enable me to enter the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s vows.
Relying on the compassionate power of the Buddha, all transgressions shall be extinguished and the pure causes of liberation shall increase.
When the time of death approaches, one will know for oneself that the hour has come;
the body will not suffer pain, and the mind will be free from attachment.
With my mind undisturbed and free from distraction, as if entering meditative absorption,
the Buddha and the assembly of sages shall come to welcome me, holding golden platforms in their hands;
in the space of a single thought-moment, I shall be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Upon the blossoming of the flower, one sees the Buddha and immediately hears the Buddha-vehicle.
Instantly opening the Buddha-wisdom, one extensively delivers sentient beings and fulfills the vow for Bodhi. Having made this vow, one should then cease;
it is not necessary to prostrate.
One must not abandon this for even a single day throughout this entire life;
by simply ensuring that one does not abandon it, one will cause the mind to be born in that land.
Third is the gate of binding the object of focus.
Whenever the Master visited private residences for nourishment or engaged in various affairs,
even in moments of haste, he never failed to keep the Buddha and the Pure Land in mind within his heart.
It was as if a worldly person were preoccupied with a matter of vital importance.
Although one undergoes various activities such as speaking, coming and going, sitting and reclining, and performing diverse tasks,
it does not hinder the secret recollection of previous events, which remains vividly present;
the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha should likewise be so.
Alternatively, if one loses mindfulness, one repeatedly gathers it back;
after a long time, this becomes one's nature, such that one spontaneously and constantly maintains mindfulness.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:

For example, it is like two people who are each single-mindedly mindful of one another: one person constantly thinking of sentient beings is like the Buddha always keeping sentient beings in mind, and one person single-mindedly recollecting is like sentient beings recollecting the Buddha; when these two people are mindful of each other, their mutual mindfulness becomes profound. It is just so.
From birth to birth, they remain like a form and its shadow, never diverging from one another.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child;
yet if the child runs away and hides, what can even that remembrance accomplish?
If a child remembers its mother as the mother remembers the child,
then throughout successive lives, mother and child shall not be separated or far apart.
If the minds of sentient beings remember the Buddha and contemplate the Buddha, [they shall likewise never be parted].
In this present life or in the future, they will certainly see the Buddha and will not be far from him;
without relying on expedient means, their minds will spontaneously open.
It is like a person who has been smeared with incense, whose body retains its fragrance.
In this way, by binding the mind, one spontaneously and constantly wards off all evil thoughts;
even if one should wish to commit an evil act,
it is prevented by the recollection of the Buddha.
Evil cannot be accomplished.
Even when one follows evil and performs evil deeds, the mind remains constantly soft and pliant;
just as a body with fragrance naturally leaves behind its stench.
Furthermore, whenever a slight evil thought arises in the mind, one should immediately recollect the Buddha;
by the power of the Buddha, the evil thought will naturally subside,
just as when a person encounters a perilous situation.
By seeking such powerful assistance, one will surely be able to escape.
Furthermore, when seeing others undergoing suffering,
one should, with a mind mindful of the Buddha, take pity upon them and vow that they may be free from suffering.
If one administers criminal justice, because of the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, one should give rise to a mind of compassion.
Although acting in accordance with the royal law, one should secretly make this vow:
"I am carrying out the royal law, but it is not my original intention."
One should vow to be born in the Pure Land and pledge to rescue one another.
Whenever one encounters any state of existence, whether wholesome or unwholesome, one should,
by recollecting the Buddha in the mind, bring it to mind and make this vow.
Therefore, the King of Vows of Samantabhadra states:
"All evil deeds shall not succeed;
all virtuous karmas shall be fully harmonized."
It is precisely this mind that is so;
thus, when mindfulness of the Buddha continues in this manner within the mind,
it is able to accomplish all meritorious qualities that are causes for purification.
Fearing that it would weary the reader, I shall not explain it in full detail here.
Truly, this gateway is of the greatest benefit.
Fourth, the clarification of the gateway of manifold merits:
The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states:
"If a king or a high minister wishes to repent of grave offenses,
they should practice five matters."
First, one should simply rectify the mind, refrain from slandering the Triple Gem, and not obstruct those who leave the household life.
One should not create evil obstacles for those practicing the Brahma-faring life, nor should one commit defiling acts against the fourfold assembly who uphold the precepts.
Second, to filially support one’s parents and serve one’s teachers and elders;
third, to govern the state according to the True Dharma and not oppress the people with injustice or corruption;
fourth, on the six days of fasting (ṣaḍ-upoṣadha), to issue commands throughout all territories within one’s domain.
To the extent of one's power, one should cause the practice of non-killing to be observed, strictly prohibit fishing and hunting, and admonish against adultery and fighting.
Regarding the six days of fasting (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*),
on the eighth day of the waxing moon, the messengers of the Four Heavenly Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*) patrol the world.
On the fourteenth day, the princes of the Four Kings conduct their inspection;
on the fifteenth day, the Four Great Heavenly Kings personally conduct their inspection;
during the dark fortnight, they inspect the world on the twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days.
Following the sequence of the waxing moon as described above, it concludes and begins again.
If the Four Heavenly Kings descend in person, all the stars, constellations, ghosts, and spirits will follow them simultaneously.
Should they encounter those who cultivate merit through fasting and the observance of precepts, [they shall protect them].
The various devas rejoice together;
they immediately bestow longevity and increase the life-span of this person,
protecting their meritorious deeds so that they may be brought to fulfillment.
Fifth, one should have deep faith in cause and effect,
believing in the Single True Path and knowing that the Buddha does not perish.
This is largely identical to the "Three Kinds of Meritorious Conduct" in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations Sutra).
However, because the *Universal Worthy Contemplation Sutra* was specifically intended for kings and ministers,
this [text] is particularly cited from it;
furthermore, it is the primary cause for the pure lands of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
If one belongs to the fourfold assembly of the ordained, one should practice by fully relying on the three types of merit described in the *Contemplation Sūtra*.
One should personally examine the text and perform at least one of these merits;
furthermore, they must be performed immediately, whether through mental recollection or verbal expression.
Only through mental attention and dedication does it become a pure cause.
Therefore, you who are exhorted to practice must, regarding these four types of Dharma-gates,
bind yourself to them daily and cultivate them with single-minded devotion.
Only then may one set for oneself the expectation of certain rebirth in the Pure Land.
These four practices constitute the primary cause for learning the Samādhi of Buddha-recollection and attaining rebirth there.
As the Sūtra says:
One who practices this samādhi will,
in their present body, behold Amitābha Buddha and the two bodhisattvas.
If a person merely hears the name of the Buddha and the names of the two bodhisattvas, [they shall likewise attain this].
It eternally eliminates the sins of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas;
how much more so for those who maintain mindfulness! If there are those who recite the Buddha's name, [they shall attain liberation].
You should know that such a person is a *puṇḍarīka* lotus among men,
with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta as their supreme friends.
When they sit at the site of enlightenment, they shall be born into the family of all Buddhas. In this present life,
that Buddha will constantly dispatch countless transformation Buddhas, countless transformation Avalokiteśvaras, and transformation Mahāsthāmaprāptas.
Furthermore, twenty-five bodhisattvas constantly protect this Sahā world day and night;
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, at all times and in all places,
they ensure that malevolent spirits find no opportunity to cause harm.
They shall not suffer any calamities;
they will always be revered by kings, ministers, and all the people;
and such shall be the merit they obtain.
In a single thought-moment it is beyond calculation;
even the eloquence of a Buddha could not fully extol it,
with the exception of those who are unworthy.
Who, upon hearing this, would not believe and rejoice?
